speaker: The Chairman
text: Head T, the Ministry of National Development (MND).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Deputy Chair Xie Yao Quan will share some ideas around the design of the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) programme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Member Liang Eng Hwa will call for MND to scale up on the Age Well neighborhoods and Community Care Apartments, and for added support for Town Councils as Town Councils cope with rising cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Member Ang Wei Neng will talk about improving Build-To-Order (BTO) housing accessibility for singles, private estate residents and raising the income ceiling beyond $14,000.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Member Foo Cexiang will advocate for relaxing Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat purchase restrictions for Singaporeans with non-resident spouses and introducing a flexible short-lease scheme for seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Member Nadia Samdin will provide suggestions on how to improve the diversity of our housing topology and how we can improve our city in nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Member Cai Yinzhou will speak about creating third spaces in communities, how we can reimagine homeownership for all, and how we can adapt HDBs to last longer beyond 99 years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As for myself, I will speak on three areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How we can make housing more accessible and affordable, ensuring we have enough homes and land to meet rising demand and how we can strengthen our built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My first point is on increasing accessibility and affordability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our aggressive housing build since COVID-19 has enabled first-time buyers, especially those with young families to get a new flat.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have mentioned several times that these families earn too much for public rental, but they cannot secure loans due to a divorce or through past financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They end up renting rooms in others' flats, paying near-mortgage sums or even more, building no asset and no security for their children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The next group is multi-generational families who are downsizing from private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some of these families want to stay together but can no longer afford private property due to family fragmentation, business failures or financial difficulty.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If their net worth is comparable to typical HDB-dwelling families, can MND consider giving them access to 5-room BTOs immediately?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The recent BTO ramp-up has focused rightfully on smaller type flats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But with supply recovering, can MND ensure that the 5-room pipeline keeps pace with this demand?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The income ceiling has not kept pace with rising wages and property, especially condominium prices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many capable Singaporeans who do well might want to have a reasonable cost of living, especially against a backdrop of uncertainty in employment in the future, and they want a HDB rather than a condominium.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sixth, more executive condominiums (ECs) and more affordable ECs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope we can do more, but simply upping the grant may not help if the developers simply adjust the prices upward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, if the Government is prepared to do more, I hope we can also include other measures like extending our minimum occupation period (MOP) or introducing profit-sharing mechanisms upon resale before MOP.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Moving beyond HDB, we should also pay attention to the many ageing private condominiums.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of these older development condominiums face insufficient sinking funds and outdated infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope MND can consider providing targeted support where there is funding assistance for lift replacements, upgrading or maintenance, or providing funds for senior-friendly upgrades.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: MND should also ensure Management Corporations Strata Title (MCSTs), moving forward, set adequate reserves early and review how MCSTs are governed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My second point is to ensure that we build enough homes, but more importantly, we must find enough land.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am delighted that MND intends to sustain aggressive build schedules that has continued since COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because if we relaxed BTO criteria, as what I have argued, demand will rise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And beyond this policy-driven demand, our underlying demand is also rising.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Just look around, you are seeing more family fragmentations, more Singaporeans living longer, more singles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And critically, supply confidence matters as much as supply itself.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: During COVID-19, fear of waiting triggered more panic-buying.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I support MND's commitment to maintain a ready stock of flats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Where are we going to find the land?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, we already devoted 15% of our land to housing, and this is against other competing demands for our small island state.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And this 15% does not even include the infrastructure, the parks, the roads and the shops within the housing estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And there is only, I think, three answers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It means more lift lobbies, higher-specification lifts, more stringent fire safety requirements, higher lift maintenance that Town Councils must bear, and I certainly hope that MND can help with that cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It cannot be rolled out too fast, too aggressively.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The second way is beyond building higher is that we must find more land to be freed up, and we must be very candid with this trade-off.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If we are determined to keep housing accessible and affordable, then that same determination must also be matched by our willingness to identify and release suitable greenfield and brownfield sites in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As a Member of Kebun Baru, bordering the Central Nature Reserve, I have seen, in person, how carefully MND engages conservation groups and residents when land, greenfield sites is being freed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, when I first became a Member of Parliament (MP), there was this area within my estate, Teachers Estate, it is a whole greenfield site, that was being transformed to the Lentor Hills development area today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The MND officers and I went on 23 engagements.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We consulted experts, we talked to different groups of people and got everybody's comfort before we proceeded with development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And my personal experience showed that MND has struck the right balance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, I hope we have the determination to find more land to build more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But at the same time, as we free up more land, we must also actively replace the lost greenery through new parks, ecological corridors and sustained tree-planting.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I recall that the Million Trees campaign, I believe during COVID-19, former-MND Minister Desmond planted the first tree in Botanic Gardens, and then the first row of trees started in Kebun Baru in Avenue 4, just in front of our Community Centre.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, I hope that this Million Trees campaign showed what is possible, and as we build more homes, I hope MND and the National Parks Board (NParks) can consider a follow-up effort, maybe the next Million Trees campaign, so that housing growth and greenery growth can continue together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Speaking to residents recently, one suggestion came up consistently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: HDB should offer residents, especially those above 50, the option of a same room-type replacement flat with perhaps a shorter lease, so they do not need to find cash to top-up for a new flat.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This would increase support for VERS so that we can free up more land.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My final part is about the built sector and MND being pro-enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This coincides with continued tightening of foreign manpower policies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A challenging combination, especially if we want to keep manpower and construction costs manageable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I welcome an update from MND on how our digitisation and productivity efforts, particularly building information modelling adoption and pre-fabrication are progressing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, let me talk about MND being pro-enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) Conference in January this year which I attended, Minister Chee signalled that MND would work with the industry to streamline its processes and be more pro-enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Among the participants, I noted that his remark was very well received.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, can MND give a preview of this plan about how MND can be more pro-enterprise?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What unites these responsibilities is that they shape the daily lives of Singaporeans – the homes we return to, the parks we walk in and the neighbourhoods we build our future in.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pritam Singh, you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members of the House would have come across many young Singaporean couples looking forward to starting a family and buying their first HDB BTO flat, but for one reason or another are unable to do so or unable to secure a flat of their choice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the HDB resale market does not impose any income ceiling, Singaporeans, in general, and young families in particular, remain concerned about lease decay, retirement adequacy and, in many cases, missing out on the taxpayer subsidies that come with BTO flat purchases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, for the new generation of Singaporeans, the property escalator of their parents' generation has become a Singapore story of the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many wage earners cannot aspire like their parents did in the context of moving from a HDB flat to a condominium and to a landed property.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: HDB flats will continue to house the majority of Singaporeans, with the financial commitment of new private homes, in particular, including ECs, representing a more significant financial outlay than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Significantly though, a new reality is setting in for newer generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The jobs environment for young people and middle-aged workers is increasingly unpredictable and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, younger and middle-aged, Singaporeans are concerned about being made redundant by the rapid advance of technology and job redesign.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who seek to purchase HDB BTO flats, these realities factor into their thinking when they consider property purchases, which have to be financed for the long term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A couple's combined income may be on the higher end or even surpassed the income ceiling threshold to varying degrees today, but that may not be so tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so if a spouse loses their job or decides to dedicate his or her life to raising children or looking after aged parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the last few years, HDB has introduced a number of policy levers to make BTO flats more affordable, partly arising from galloping resale prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One example is the subsidy clawback regime which started at around 6% and is now at 14% for some BTO developments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other is the extension of the MOP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is at least one HDB scheme that imposes an MOP of 20 years although this scheme is one that transits rental home dwellers to a HDB flat on a longer lease.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as the income eligibility criteria would be adjusted regularly for the majority of buyers, this would effectively remove the income eligibility ceiling for a small category of buyers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To ensure fairness, should this first-timer couple seek to purchase such a BTO flat, these flats can be encumbered with one or more additional requirements, such as: the purchase ought to be restricted to the first matrimonial home, requiring an age cap of either spouse to be 35 years and below; including a longer MOP than that set out for that particular category of BTO flats be they Plus, Prime or Standard; and/or include an additional subsidy clawback mechanism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With eight out of 10 Singaporean households covered by the existing income ceiling, the provision of an additional option to buy a new BTO flat with encumbrances to first-time young Singaporeans is unlikely to require the construction of a significantly larger number of BTO flats than it is already planned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it can give significant peace of mind to some Singaporeans for whom the jobs environment of the future is less certain that it was for previous generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2004, the HDB introduced the Facade Repairs Co-payment Scheme where HDB would fund facade-related repairs and reimburse Town Councils for repair works done to damaged facade of HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was increased to 75% for blocks with brick cladding and some metal fixtures under a special enhancement programme that runs from 2023 to 2028 for blocks with a higher risk of facade failure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, water seepage that emanates from the block facade into a resident's unit is not covered by any co-funding scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the HDB stock continues to age, the prospect of water seepage, especially from the facade of older blocks, anecdotally appears to be on the rise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would HDB reach out to assist Town Councils through the Facade Repairs Co-payment Scheme to allow for the inclusion of claims to be made for water seepage cases that originate from the block facade?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taken together, these moves may contribute to more prudent bidding although it remains open to question what impact it would have on shops located in areas of high footfall.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The majority of HDB shops are in private hands, 8,500 compared to 7,000 rented out by the HDB.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative will provide the public with assurance that effective measures are being taken to address rental issues faced by fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, council members will be positioned to identify potential money laundering activities, particularly in cases of unusually high rental payments.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, at the COS debates back in 2023 and the debate on the HDB (Amendment) Bill in the same year, I raised my concerns about the uneven distribution of hawker centres and coffee shops across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fast forward to 2026, Sengkang finally had its own hawker centres, with Buangkok opening in 2023 and Anchorvale Village in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the completion of Rivervale Shores, the entire Rivervale division with 18,000 or so households finally had more than one coffee shop.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The MND shared in an earlier COS response that most residents can access commercial facilities with a food court or an eating house within 400 metres from their homes or an approximately five to 10 minutes' walk.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The question then is, what is the percentage of residents that have to travel more than 400 metres to access a food court or an eating house?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that new BTO projects do contain retail and F&B options, there remains spanning neighbourhoods within and outside that do not.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A case in point is the value meals at Southwest Project that was launched in March 2025 which aimed to place 80 vending machines in heartland locations for residents to purchase.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Subsequently, such vending machines were also installed in Punggol and to quote Deputy Prime Minister Gan, he hoped to deploy more such vending machines across Punggol for the convenience of our residents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Sengkang, after the projected period of working with the HDB and external vendors, we finally have hot-food vending machines, cafes, across three locations: at 108 Rivervale Walk, 188C Rivervale Drive and 288B Compassvale Crescent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am grateful for the vendor, which is a replacement vendor after the initial vendor pulled out, for the commitment to the project despite the various challenges faced, chief of which is uncertainty around demand and the high fixed and overhead cost incurred.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than the ad hoc projects being introduced in Punngol, Sengkang or any other town, I hope the HDB can consider a large-scale tender of multiple sites across HDB towns to ensure that affordable and accessible meals are available to all residents across Singapore, especially those which currently do not have a food court or an eating house within 400 metres from their homes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would then provide for sufficient economies of scale for would-be operators, allowing them to have greater business sustainability and visibility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, any incremental rental revenue derived by HDB should not be a primary consideration, given that the physical footprint of a vending machine is small and the vacant void deck space would not have been revenue-generating in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, there is no issue of opportunity cost for HDB.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the MMD to consider extending similar initiatives island-wide, similar to how it has piloted the Pick Locker Network island wide across HDB void decks for the convenience of all residents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Affordable food access should not depend on which district one lives in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, the price of ECs in Singapore has skyrocketed in the past 10 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: ECs are touted as a more affordable option for young couples who desire to purchase a private condo but not have the means to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Understandably, the price per square foot for an EC will be higher than a resale HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Well, I will argue that the prices today have become too expensive to service the original intention.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As ECs were slated as a more premium yet affordable public-private hybrid for prospective buyers, its premiums can be compared to the resale market for HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These numbers would differ, of course, based on the type of neighbourhood that the HDB flats and ECs are located.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Well, for the sake of comparison, they do serve as a useful broad basis for comparison.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The difference is even more stark in absolute terms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at the average price of a new EC in 2016, this stood at around $860,000 versus $439,000 for a resale HDB flat, a difference of around $421,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the EC housing scheme was introduced in 1996, then-MND Minister Mr Lim Hng Kiang stated that the sharp increases in private property prices in the last few years had again created a sandwiched class of young people who are beyond HDB's income ceiling, but who cannot afford private property.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From 2021 to 2025, only four in 10 EC purchases were first-timers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even so, I reckon one has to have access to the deep pockets of one's parents if one is lucky, without which a first-timer will find it very challenging to fork out the downpayment required to afford the EC in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the irony is that based on current financing rules, young people who are currently unable to afford an EC are deemed to be able to afford and purchase and even higher price private condominium.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is because the ECs are subject to a 30% mortgage servicing ratio while private condominiums are only subject to the 55% total debt servicing ratio.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At a prevailing household income ceiling of $16,000 per month, prospective EC buyers will be able to secure a loan of close to $1 million based on an mortgage servicing ratio of 30%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it does not address the fundamental issue of affordability since the price of the EC itself will not be impacted.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With affordability and equitable access being key tenets to underpin the new EC model.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That mission has become increasingly complicated as Singaporean households take on different structures and HDB needs to assess how to apportion taxpayer subsidies and grants in a myriad of different situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some form families later in life, others prioritise multi-generational caregiving, all while following life and career paths that are not always linear.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One area that I wish to raise for review is the imposition of the MOP on non-owners that is on the listed occupiers of a flat.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a policy can cause hardship to families in certain situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, a widowed or divorced middle-aged parent may want to downsize and decides to purchase a subsidised 3-room flat, listing an unmarried adult child as an essential occupier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under HDB's policies, the MOP period will apply to both owners and occupiers alike.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a restriction on the unmarried adult children who are only occupiers will restrict their life choice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If they later meet a life partner but defer marriage for another five to 10 years, this could take them out of their critical child-bearing years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our housing policy should not inadvertently discourage younger Singaporeans who wish to start families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But as family structures and life courses of Singaporeans become more diverse, our public housing policies need to be responsive to such lived realities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I urge the Ministry to continue to consider how existing rules and frameworks can be better refined to align with these diverse aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As HDB supply ramps up to meet demand, we must move beyond merely providing "roofs over heads" to refining the inclusivity of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I ask the Ministry for clarity on how it will prioritise five key areas.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it time to recalibrate income ceilings to reflect today's wage realities?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The 15-month wait-out period was a necessary cooling measure, but for families and citizens in life transitions, it remains a blunt instrument.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we move toward a more nuanced, case-based approach to facilitate downsizing?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many young Singaporeans are pursuing non-traditional life paths.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, Singaporeans with foreign spouses often face more restrictive pathways to home ownership.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Housing stability for these families in a globalised environment is a matter of long-term domestic stability for our own citizens.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I ask the Ministry to consider a more sympathetic prioritisation based on the child's age and to equalise subsidies so that every child, regardless of family structure, starts life in a secure environment.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us dare to imagine a Singapore where affordable housing is not just available to some, but truly accessible, at the right price and the right size, for all.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, I want to propose improving pathways for home ownership for households currently living in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister, in his Budget debate round-up speech, mentioned the importance of enabling Singaporeans to accumulate assets.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As he said, asset ownership gives families a concrete stake in our nation's success and allows them to share directly in Singapore's progress.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Imagine a family of five in a rental flat.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Month after month, they pay subsidised rent but build nothing – no home equity, no assets to pass down.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is a reality for thousands of families in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For a nation where 90% own their homes and home equity makes up over half of household wealth, families living in rental flats need a leg-up on the ladder of opportunity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Apart from rental flat to home ownership, from shelter to security and from surviving to thriving.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: First, I am proposing that the Ministry focus on helping more rental households achieve home ownership.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In May 2021, then-Minister Desmond Lee shared in a Parliamentary response that only 2% of rental households transition to home ownership each year.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For those who do make this transition, this journey takes considerable time.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Another third, take between five and 10 years.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A further third managed it in under five years, while fewer than one in 10 succeed within three years.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am hopeful that these numbers have improved since then, thanks to enhancements made to programmes like the Enhanced Housing Grant, the Step Up CPF Housing Grant and the Fresh Start Housing Scheme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I also recognise the dedicated efforts of the HDB Home Ownership Support Team and the coordinated support provided through ComLink+ across multiple agencies.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Minister: what targets has the Minister set to increase the number of rental households transitioning to home ownership for each year, up to 2030?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And what strategies is the Ministry pursuing to shorten the time it takes for families to move from public rental housing into their own homes?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My second proposal is a shared equity pilot programme to help families achieve home ownership sooner.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Right now, families may want to buy a home and may meet key social agency assessments, but they are stuck because they cannot afford the cash or Central Provident Fund (CPF) down payment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even with HDB grants, it takes years of steady work and savings to build up that initial sum for down payment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: During this time, families miss out getting on the home ownership ladder and building equity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The pilot will target young families, 35 and under, currently in rental housing, as well as young adults in public rental flats who apply for another rental unit when they start their own families.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This will reduce both the upfront cost and the loan needed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The family still pays monthly mortgage instalments, just like any homeowner.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Over time, as their finances improve, they can buy back the Government's share in stages.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If they eventually sell the flat, the Government receives its percentage of the sale price.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Unlike rent-to-purchase models, this approach lets families own a new home and build assets early.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, can HDB consider redirecting the rental payments of these households towards offsetting the cost of the new flat if they want to buy it?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must help yet more young families from challenging backgrounds break the cycle of rental housing and participate actively in building stable home ownership, valuable equity and long-term wealth alongside Singapore's growth.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, 85.9% of senior households wish to continue living in their existing flats rather than move.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The number of single person households is increasing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In 2023, 15.6% of the 1.1 million households living in HDB flats were single person households, up from 12.6% in 2018.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In absolute terms, this is more than 30,000 additional solo households in just five years.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must understand what this means in practical terms.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Most of today's seniors are baby boomers born between 1946 and 1964.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: They would have married in their mid-20s and moved into new flats in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These flats are now close to 50 years old.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Entire towns, such as Bedok, Ang Mo Kio and Marine Parade, reflect this reality – mature estates with ageing flats and ageing residents with more and more living alone.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As these seniors age alongside their homes, they must cope with ageing electrical systems, plumbing issues, worn fittings and outdated appliances.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is something that I have seen first-hand during house visits in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) programme and the Home Improvement Programme (HIP) exist to help seniors stay safe and mobile at home, the programme only provide subsidies rather than cash support to help seniors continue living safely and comfortably in their older flats.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, even if the repairs might not be a major cost from our perspectives, it can be a moderate burden that weighs heavy on the minds of our seniors living alone.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The key challenge before us is not simply longevity, but quality of life, ensuring that our seniors can age well, age with active social life and healthy living within their own communities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The aim is to enable seniors to age with dignity within their communities, offering services like home fixes, health checks, social activities while staying integrated, not isolated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Features, such as barrier-free access, therapeutic gardens, senior-friendly wayfinding, fitness corners with low-impact equipment and co-location of health and social services are meaningful improvements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I welcome MND's plans to redesign our older estates so that seniors can age comfortably in place and to remain active and socially connected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Toa Payoh will be among the first town to have Age Well Neighbourhood and I look forward to Minister sharing the broader implementation plan across the island.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I also ask the Minister to share how is MND working with the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) to integrate community care, active ageing centres and primary care services within these neighbourhoods?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Beyond physical infrastructure, ageing-in-place also depends on social infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Seniors who remain socially connected tend to enjoy better health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope MND can elaborate on how town design will facilitate inter-generational interactions, for example, through shared community spaces, programming nodes and proximity to childcare centres or schools.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Community Care Apartments are an important innovation in public housing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They integrate senior-friendly design with care services, communal spaces and emergency response systems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Demand has been encouraging and many seniors appreciate the combination of independence and support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Bukit Panjang, we are seeing growing interest among seniors who wish to right-size from larger flats while remaining near their children and social networks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many value the familiar environment and established amenities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, may I ask the Minister: what is the projected supply of Community Care Apartments over the next five years?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How does MND assess demand across different towns and how quickly can supply be ramped up, if take-up remains strong?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Will future Community Care Apartments explore more flexible care packages to cater to seniors with differing levels of needs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As our population ages, housing policy must evolve alongside healthcare and community care systems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The goal should be to create neighbourhoods where seniors can transition seamlessly across stages of ageing – from independent living, to supported living, to higher levels of care – without needing to uproot themselves from their familiar surroundings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, the integration of Age Well Neighbourhoods and Community Care Apartments presents a holistic model.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One strengthens the broader environment; the other provides targeted housing solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Together, they can anchor a comprehensive ecosystem for ageing-in-place.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even as we continue building new BTO flats, a growing proportion of our HDB stock is ageing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the coming years, more flats will cross the 30-year mark.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With ageing estates come higher maintenance demands, not just more frequent repairs, but more complex and costly rectification works.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Town Councils are facing sustained cost pressures on multiple fronts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Tender prices for conservancy services have increased significantly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Contractors have cited higher labour costs from the Progressive Wage Model, higher foreign worker accommodation costs and tighter operating conditions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Other essential services have also seen steep increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, pest control costs for crows, pigeons and rodents have trended upwards.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Horticulture contracts have risen by as much as 60% and seepage repair costs by up to 32%.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are core services necessary to keep estates safe, clean and liveable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, beyond the rising cost trend, ageing infrastructure also requires heavier intervention.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While programmes by MND, such as the HIP and Neighbourhood Renewal Programme, have been extremely helpful, the bulk of day-to-day estate maintenance remains the responsibility of Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Works, such as external wall seepage repairs, lift maintenance and upgrading, re-roofing, external rewiring, replacement of lighting systems and structural and façade rectification, are becoming more frequent and more intensive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Town Councils are also concerned about the long-term maintenance implications of the Pneumatic Waste Conveyance System.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While there was initial subsidy support, this is not intended to be permanent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, over time, operating and maintenance costs will have to be absorbed within Town Council's budgets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These cumulative pressures inevitably impact Town Councils' finances and, in turn, will have a bearing on the service and conservancy charges (S&CC) paid by residents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That support was very helpful, but it has since expired.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, on behalf of the People's Action Party (PAP) Town Councils, I thank MND and HDB for this significant support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But notwithstanding that, I would still like to appeal for further review of the funding framework.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Chairman, Town Councils are committed to maintaining clean, safe and well-managed estates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Residents rightly expect high standards, but S&CC must also remain affordable, especially for lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The Minister said recently, in response to Parliamentary Questions, that VERS should not create a "lottery effect" nor end up becoming a wealth-generating programme for affected homeowners.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Today, I would like to advocate for an opposite point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: While VERS should not create a windfall for affected homeowners, it should also not short-change them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: All affected homeowners should get a fair deal, fair compensation, from VERS.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Flats acquired under VERS will be 70 years or older generally.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, with leases of 29 years or less remaining.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The market value of these leases will be modest and may well turn out to be insufficient to match the price or market value of a replacement flat that is completely new, of similar type and with lease covering the affected homeowner until at least 95 years old.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In such a scenario, affected homeowners would ordinarily have to make a cash top-up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And obviously, such a subsidy, such a scheme, will require the Government to utilise more fiscal resources than what is needed to simply acquire property leases at market value.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What would be a fair size to this subsidy?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What would be a fair valuation of fairness to current, affected homeowners?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The Government will need to use sound and consistent principles for such an exercise, to justify the higher public spending that this implies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: One plausible principle, to my mind, is that there is simply a fair cost to orderly urban renewal, beyond the cost of property.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: There is a cost to relocating lives, resettling lives, especially because it may well be involuntary for some even if it is voluntary for most.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In this way, the Government will be fair to all homeowners.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Diminishing lease is a genuine concern for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: I urge the Ministry to shift the narrative from flats of stored value depreciating.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: This means ensuring every Singaporean, regardless of age or ability, to live in the same home through every life stage of changing needs, with dignity and security.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: I have four proposals to make in this reality.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Has the Ministry studied increasing the list of modification options during upgrading?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: For multi-generational families, this could include space partitioning and soundproofing.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: And extending EASE to supporting families with persons with special needs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Can we expand HIP to include built-in for fall-detection sensors, fire sprinklers and emergency alert buttons?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Third, for the most vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Will Ministry consider resources for public rental flats to be more climate resilient, noting that they are space constrained and structurally disadvantaged for natural ventilation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: If education is the great social leveler, then study space is essential equitable infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: In a cramped two-room rental flat with six children, there is no quiet corner or dedicated desk for one, let alone six children.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: As suggested during the Budget debate, it could stand for Adaptable, Compact, Child-centric, Enhancements for Small Spaces.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: If we truly believe in social mobility, we must prioritise the design of the space where that mobility begins.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Homes for Life is more than a slogan, but about ensuring our residents feel secure in the longevity of their community, where they do not just have a roof over their heads, but a place where their roots can grow with confidence.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: My late grandmother lived at Old Airport Road, where her life and friendships were deeply rooted.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: In 2014, when nearby Dakota Crescent residents were told to move, I founded Dakota Adventures, co-guiding tours with senior residents for over 1,500 Singaporeans, including hon Minister Grace Fu.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: In 2017, then-Minister Lawrence Wong announced the conservation of six blocks, out of 15, to allow future generations to build their memories.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: We need a more robust and local framework for urban renewal.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: This would allow us to proactively reimagine existing spaces rather than retrospectively conserving them.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: And also, to account for the heritage and social impact that potential relocation might have towards, especially, the seniors living in those estates.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Furthermore, our ABC Waterways network spans 8,000 kilometres through our homes and communities.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: I hope the Ministry can move beyond aesthetic "water views" as a mode of promotion and instead, incorporate active "blue spaces" for recreational activities, like water sports and fishing, and even consider exploring water-based transportation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Chairman, I look forward to a vision for a more social- and heritage-conscious urban landscape that truly reflects the social value of landmarks, like Dakota Crescent, which remains hoarded up today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During my Adjournment Motion in January, I spoke about the urgent need to rethink our approach to green preservation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In response, the Minister of State characterised the Serangoon River Forest site as a former landfill, regenerated vegetation and comprising of, "young, exotic-dominated secondary forest, scrubland, grassland and ponds." I have since received feedback from a resident, Ms Han Sai Por, who articulated a point at the heart of this policy gap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: She said that the disagreement is not about the intent to be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is about the valuation of our land, the problem with static planning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our current planning system is heavily anchored in the past.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If a site was a landfill in 1998 or zoned as a reserve site decades ago, that historical classification seems to override the biological reality of 2026.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet, over the last 25 years, nature has reclaimed these spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The secondary forest, while not primary, now provide frontline climate resilience, riverbank stabilisation, run-off filtration and significant urban cooling for dense neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must move away from a purely species-centric lands that dismisses young forests to a resident worried about the urban heat island effect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The cooling services are not lesser because the trees are non-native.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some countries are starting to put the revitalisation of brownfield sites as a nature-based solution strategy high on their policy agenda.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is it time we start doing the same?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does our current planning framework sufficiently value these re-generated ecosystems?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How is the ecosystem service value, such as flood regulation and heat mitigation, quantified when deciding whether to clear a site?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, the public often only sees the results of an environmental impact assessments (EIA) once a project is decided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We rarely see the screening process that concludes that an EIA is unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, even back in 1990, Prof Tommy Koh had, in the forward for the Nature Society of Singapore's Master Plan for the Conservation of Nature in Singapore, expressed hope that, "All development projects in Singapore will require an environmental impact assessment." I call on MND to consolidate its assessment framework into two mandatory commitments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, integrated baseline and functional assessments, where the Ministry commit to conducting a baseline study for all forested plots, regardless of zoning, that evaluate both biodiversity and functional climate roles, including heat mitigation and flood absorption, before any development decision is finalised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Ministry mandate an EIA and include clearer thresholds for duration of fallow status and site size?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For a start, studies have shown that a brownfield site can become ecologically important within five to 10 years and become significant mature ecosystems after another 10 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even small sites between point-one and point-five hectares can become ecologically meaningful in the same time period, depending on their function and location.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Crucially, if the Government decides an EIA is not needed, can the Ministry publish the assessment and scientific rationale?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet too often, we jump straight to mitigate, for example, using noise barriers or phased clearing while avoid is treated as a foregone conclusion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A case in point is the current bus depot construction at the Serangoon River Forest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must exhaustively evaluate alternatives, such as multi-storey industrial depots and existing transport nodes before touching our remaining green buffers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The lift upgrading programme was launched by HDB in 2001 to provide residents with lift access to every floor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this year's COS, I am asking once again for same floor lift access for all residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is a fundamental issue of equity, safety and dignity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As our population ages, a few steps become a daily insurmountable wall, separating seniors and those with mobility challenges from their community and essential services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: HDB's common reply to my many appeal letters to HDB, on behalf of residents, without same floor lift access in the past few years, was that such blocks are not eligible for Lift Upgrading Programme (LUP) due to high cost and/or technical constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In Hougang, recent breakthroughs are both welcome and puzzling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In 2023, HDB started work on offering LUP for Block 833 Hougang Central.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In September 2025, HDB offered LUP to the remaining units at Block 363 Hougang Avenue 5.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Affected residents at the remaining Blocks 830, 831, 832 and 835 have wondered why did HDB offered LUP to remaining units of Blocks 833 and 363, but not their blocks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: No reasons have been offered by HDB for their change of minds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: May we know which are these blocks and how soon will LUP be awarded?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With a clear roadmap, residents in the remaining blocks will not be in a state of anxious limbo.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These architectural barriers result from an outdated design before the mid-90s.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, during a recent house visit, one affected Block 832 resident told me that at the time of choosing the unit, they were not told that it did not come with same floor lift access, unlike other units in the same block.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let the residents know as soon as possible HDB's LUP plans for them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Former Hougang MP Mr Png Eng Huat, had said in this House previously, to the effect that why were the affected blocks not combined with other neighbouring blocks in previous bulk LUP projects in the earlier days, instead of tendering difficult blocks for LUP by themselves later on?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The former could have been more cost effective, not to mention that LUP costs would have been lower, say, 10 to 15 years ago or definitely before COVID?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While we understand the cost constraints, we hope HDB will continue to study new engineering solutions and emerging technologies to extend lift access to these remaining blocks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A significant number of affected blocks are in Nanyang and many residents continue to face daily accessibility challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many households in these segmented units bought their flats more than 30 years ago, when direct lift access on every floor was not the norm.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In their younger days, they were mobile and valued the added privacy due to the design of the flat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But today, as they age, climbing stairs several times a day before they can take the lift has become increasingly difficult and, for some, unsafe.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is ultimately about ageing in place, dignity and inclusive public housing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If LUP remains unfeasible for these blocks, I respectfully suggest that HDB consider several policy adjustments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, households typically need medical certification that an occupier is wheelchair-bound or has serious mobility limitations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Earlier intervention can prevent hardship, rather than respond only after mobility has significantly deteriorated.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Where owners of segmented flats wish to sell, HDB could study the feasibility of buy-back at market value and engage JTC or other agencies to lease out to tenants who are better able to manage walk-up access.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This may help avoid a recurring cycle where future elderly residents face the same accessibility constraints.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If buy-back is not viable, HDB may wish to require clear disclosure to prospective buyers that these flats are unlikely to benefit from LUP in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This ensures buyers make informed decisions and avoid unrealistic expectations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Chairman, residents in these 100 blocks are not asking for special treatment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are asking for a fair chance to age safely and independently in their own homes, just like what majority of HDB households would now enjoy the direct lift access.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope HDB and MND will continue to review policy options and work towards a more inclusive and age-friendly public housing system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Behind each case is a resident whose daily life has been affected.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Homes and common areas fouled by droppings and in some worrying cases, residents being attacked.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In Nanyang, we have witnessed such incidents first-hand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singaporeans support our vision of a City in Nature.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But coexistence must not come at the expense of public safety, hygiene and livability.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When disamenities persist, we must act more decisively.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Under NParks' pigeon management plan, efforts remain largely focused on pigeons.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I urge NParks, within MND's broader human-wildlife management framework, to evolve towards a comprehensive Pest Bird Management approach, one that also addresses other urban-adapted species, such as mynas and crows, where they cause persistent disamenities to residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This requires a system-wide approach: stronger enforcement against illegal bird feeding, tighter food waste control around eateries and markets, estate-level habitat management and where necessary, science-based population control.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this respect, I welcome NParks' decision to resume shooting of crows.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As his comments set out the direction forward, I will make a narrow point about culling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: NParks has been helpful to town councils, assisting in the removal of nests and the installation of temporary traps to manage the crow population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can the Ministry share its protocols with regard to culling, or specifically shooting, as a means of reducing the crow population in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When and how does it determine that the population in a given area has exceeded acceptable levels or is overpopulated with crows?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand MND has in recent months been working with the Singapore Police Force with a view to restart the shooting of crows.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What has been the result of this collaboration?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can the Minister update when such measures will be implemented across all Town Councils?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And with what frequency and what measures will also be imposed to ensure public safety?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Pigeons are not merely a nuisance, they pose genuine health risk.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: When dried droppings turn to dust, residents inhale contaminated particles that can cause severe respiratory infections, particularly affecting our elderly and immuno-compromised individuals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Beyond health concerns, residents bear the financial cost.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A constituent shared that he had to engage an air-conditioning specialist to clean his compressor unit because pigeons had defecated on it repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: He paid out of pocket for a problem not of his making.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: How many more residents are silently suffering similar inconveniences and expenses?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am concerned about the pace of the roll-out.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Residents in affected areas cannot wait indefinitely for relief.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This would allow effective solutions to be rolled out to affected estates sooner, providing residents with much needed relief.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Effective pigeon management requires Government leadership, community cooperation and adequate resources.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Our residents deserve clean, safe and hygienic living environments free from preventable health hazards and unnecessary financial burdens.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Lee Hui, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chair, animals are integral to our shared environment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The steady stream of feedback we receive on animal welfare proves that residents envision a society that is not just efficient, but harmonious and gracious.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We have come a long way, but more must be done.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The recent viral incident of a man cutting a community cat's whiskers reminds us that cruelty still lurks in the estates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As our spaces become greener, urban bird populations have risen and we have been playing a cat-and-mouse game with mother nature to manage with ecologically sensitive solutions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While pigeon population control has seen some success, we continue to face a spike in house crow populations and it affects all our residents.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Can the operations be scheduled outside school commuting hours and avoiding areas near schools and playgrounds, where young children are present?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond reactive measures, how will enforcement against illegal feeding be strengthened?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans for stepped-up surveillance in hotspots, higher penalties for repeat offenders, regular tree pruning or enhanced public education?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Can upstream measures – better waste management and environmental design – can these be strengthened to reduce reliance on shooting over time?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider conducting a Ecological Impact Assessment to study how culling efforts could affect our broader local biodiversity?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Let us act upstream, so that problems do not spiral into a full-blown "crow-sis".

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: With major infrastructure projects such as Terminal 5 underway, our construction sector continues to face significant cost and manpower pressures.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Policies must be carefully calibrated to support both workforce transformation and business sustainability.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The builders I have met, including some of my residents, have welcomed the New Action Team chaired by the Minister and they are encouraged by the strong leadership and attention placed on the sector.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What are the Ministry's long-term plans to grow infrastructure, manpower and talent pipeline to ensure supply can meet demand?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Instead of raising the salary, which permanently inflates the wage bill, not just on the foreign worker per se, the salary of other workers in the company will have to be increased accordingly.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Contractors are suggesting the increase of the workers levy instead.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This will still generate revenue for the Government without overpaying what workers ask for.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Has MND planned adequately to avoid supply chain disruptions?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For example, is there sufficient staging and dumping grounds, adequate capacity at Jurong Port to handle cement imports, and enough workers' dormitories to support projected demand?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, local talent is a matter of national resilience.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Young Singaporeans shy away from the sector due to perceptions of harsh working hours and site conditions, and our local core is ageing.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot rely solely on a transient workforce.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How will MND redesign construction careers to attract and anchor a sizable local talent pool?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This also deters locals from entering the industry.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The fear of excessive liability falling on individuals can be paralysing, but safety is non-negotiable.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, as we push digitalisation, are regulations keeping pace?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: If expect transformation, policy regulation and support must move in tandem —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is only possible through the commitment and intentionality of each generation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2020, MND launched their vision to transform Singapore into a city in nature.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have learnt since young that nature is functional.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Different species play respective roles and in the ecosystem they work together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As climate infrastructure, tree canopies and green buffer zones mitigate the urban heat island effect, lowering cooling demand and making active mobility possible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Socially, nature serves as recreational and exercise spaces, supporting mental well-being and as restorative spaces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Economically, tourists are drawn to our city in nature identity right from the time they leave the airport.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nature is the only infrastructure that cools, protects, filters and regenerates simultaneously.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many see urbanisation as the opposite of nature, but Singapore's lived experience of how we have balanced the two offers a different perspective.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is part of what makes us exceptional.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we plan it well, nature will not compete with our urban future development plans, it will secure it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, could MND share how it has weighed trade-offs and integrated nature, including preservation of existing flora and fauna into design principles for newer and upcoming housing estates towards improving heat resilience and tackling rising sea level challenges?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could NParks update on the initiatives it has undertaken to strengthen ecological connectivity and biodiversity-sensitive designs across green and blue spaces in the last five years, as well as any future plans?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we recognise that our people are joint inhabitants in our city in nature.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also means that wildlife is 10 minutes away from us, increasing the number of wildlife human interactions and sometimes clashes – from monkeys to otters, wild boars to snakes, hornbills to tapirs, sambar deer to migrating storks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And has MND assessed if the current plans, response teams and protocols remain adequate?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does MND see the long-term approach balance between containment, deterrence and co-existence?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's public housing system has also been globally recognised for delivering accessible quality housing at scale.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our homes not only provide shelter but also build communities and encourage social cohesion in estates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While home ownership rates remain fairly high compared to other cities, the focus has typically been on supporting young couples and first timers with the rising cost, which is of course, net crucial for nation building.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But population and family planning dynamics today are changing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given our ageing society, total fertility rate, marriage and divorce rates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have more singles, second timers and seniors who strongly desire to age in place.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have our public housing offerings fully adapted to these changes?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps a re-diversifying of housing typologies might need to follow to support the needs and aspirations of a changing Singapore over Singaporeans' life course.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A wider spectrum of options would allow citizens to find housing that matches not just income, but also life stage and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my earlier speeches, I have spoken on the need to better support couples and families who want to stay near or with family members.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the earlier days, a young couple who first purchases a 3-room BTO can aspire to other versions of home over the years, such as a jumbo flat, maisonette, executive apartment, or even low rise and terrace public housing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These options provide more configurations and variety of life one can look forward to beyond hacking and expanding rooms or moving from public housing to private dwellings, which can increasingly feel unattainable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, flat typologies have largely remained the same, and in fact become even more similar as we optimise for speed and scale.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How has MND reviewed the housing aspirations of Singaporeans, and can MND consider exploring some unique typologies in upcoming projects, for example, dual key or modular layout suitable for caregiving?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, for a divorcee trying to re-establish a roof over his or her head.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many experience long waiting times, high temporary rental costs and uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond schemes like Assistance Scheme for Second-Timers (ASSIST), can MND consider other forms of support for this segment to find new beginnings?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, many also support elderly parents who stay with them if there are emergencies or help with nieces and nephews on the weekend.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As both models were well subscribed, what are the plans to expand the scope of these programmes?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many rental families has the home ownership support team served over the years?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the success rates so far and are there plans to integrate —

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, housing in Singapore has never been just about putting a roof over one's head.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It has also been about giving every Singaporean a stake in the nation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this context, the directive by the Minister for National Development to build more and build faster is apt and timely.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In its addendum to the President's address last year, MND announced that HDB would review the income ceiling for BTO flats and study more housing options for singles, seniors, as well as larger families.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It also said that it would provide assistance for more rental households to transit into home ownership.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, I would like to further champion the case for two categories of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, Singaporeans with non-resident spouses with no Singaporean or permanent resident child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, this group of Singaporeans can only purchase a 2-room Flexi flat from HDB if the Singaporean is a first-timer aged 35 and above.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I seek MND's consideration to relax this requirement and allow Singaporeans with non-resident spouses and no children to purchase flats of all sizes from HDB with no minimum age for the Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to support all couples on their parenthood journey.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this regard, there has been an increasing trend of transnational citizen marriages.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a significant proportion, and as other Members of the House have raised, having a large enough home to raise a family is one of the key considerations that young couples have today when deciding whether to have a child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By restricting our Singaporean with non-resident spouses to a 2-room Flexi flat, we are constraining 25% of would-be parents from having a child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given our existential challenge, this is too high a proportion to risk.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to support all couples in their parenthood journey, including those made up of a Singaporean and a non-resident.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, seniors above 55 years old seeking to purchase a short lease, 2-room Flexi flat.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last month in Parliament, I asked if MND would consider lowering the home for life condition to require the remaining lease to cover the youngest owner till 83.5 years, which is the life expectancy age, instead of 95 years.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would enable these seniors to purchase more affordable short lease, 2-room Flexi homes, given the shorter remaining lease.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And it could be the difference between them renting their homes forever or making the transition to home ownership.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MND shared that many seniors would live longer than the average lifespan of 83.5 years, and this would compromise the home for life policy.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand the policy rationale behind setting the age at 95 to cover most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, there will be many Singaporeans who do not live to 95 years, perhaps even more so than those who do.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, my question is, will MND consider a scheme for these seniors, which allows them to purchase a short-term 2-room Flexi flat with minimum lease term that covers the youngest owner up to age 85?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And a key condition for this being that if the owners want to move out or pass away before this lease expires, the flat will be returned back to HDB with no refund or compensation to the owner or their next of kin.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These early return flats with remaining leases can then be used to house other seniors on the same scheme who live beyond 85 years and outlive their leases.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And therefore at the overall scheme level, this will be in keeping with our home for life principle.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
